articles.title: Every call has a pattern

body.support:
Are you nervous on the phone? Lots of people are. But most calls have the same **four steps**.

1. **Who.** Say your name. *Hi, my name is Jordan.*
2. **Why.** Say why you are calling. *I'm calling to book an appointment.*
3. **Check.** Answer their questions. Ask yours. Then say the details back. *So that's Tuesday at 3:45?*
4. **Close.** Say thanks and bye.

Talk **slowly**. Say numbers in small groups. Spell names that are tricky.

In a **voicemail**, say your name and number. Say why you called. Then say your number again.

In an **emergency**, call **000**. They will ask: *Police, fire or ambulance?* Then tell them **where you are**. **Stay on the line.** Do what they tell you.
body.core:
If phone calls make you nervous, you're not alone. The good news: most calls follow the same **four steps**, so you can plan them.

1. **Who.** Say your name first: *Hi, my name is Jordan Lee.*
2. **Why.** Say why you're calling in one sentence: *I'm calling to book an appointment, please.* or *I'm calling about the job ad for a kitchen hand.*
3. **Check.** Answer their questions and ask yours. Then **repeat back** the important details: *So that's Tuesday the 12th at 3:45?* This is how you catch mistakes before they matter.
4. **Close.** Thank them and say goodbye: *Great, thanks for your help. Bye.*

Your **voice** does a lot of the work. Speak a little slower than normal. Say numbers in small groups: *0412 / 345 / 678*. Spell tricky names: *That's Siobhan: S-I-O-B-H-A-N.*

**Voicemail** has its own pattern: your **name**, your **number** (slowly), **why** you called, what you'd like them to **do**, then your **number again**.

**Emergency calls (000)** are different, and you don't need to plan them, because the call-taker leads. After a recorded message, they'll ask: *Police, fire or ambulance?* Then they'll ask where you are. Give the **state and suburb or town**, then the street address, or the nearest cross street or landmark. **Stay on the line** until they tell you to hang up. They may tell you what to do while help is on the way.
body.extend:
Phone anxiety is common, partly because a call gives you no time to draft and no face to read. The fix is structure: most calls follow the same **four steps**, so you can plan them.

1. **Who.** Identify yourself first: *Hi, my name is Jordan Lee.*
2. **Why.** State your purpose in one sentence: *I'm calling about the kitchen hand job advertised on your website.*
3. **Check.** Answer and ask questions, then **paraphrase** the key details back: *So that's a trial shift Thursday at four, wearing black, and I ask for Mel?* Repeating back is how professionals catch errors.
4. **Close.** Confirm the next step, thank them and end the call politely.

Your **voice** carries meaning: pace, volume and **tone**. Slow down slightly, group numbers (*0412 / 345 / 678*), and spell names. Match your **formality** to the listener: a receptionist or manager gets *Could I please…*, not *Yeah, can I…*

**Voicemails** follow a pattern too: name, number (slowly), purpose, the action you want, and the number again.

**Emergency calls (000)** reverse the pattern, because the call-taker leads. After a recorded message, they'll ask *Police, fire or ambulance?*, then where you are: give the **state and suburb or town**, then the address, cross street or landmark. **Stay on the line** until you're told to hang up, and follow their instructions while help is on the way.

caseStudies.title: Sam stayed on the line

body.support:
In 2024, **Sam** was 16. He lives in **Warrnambool**.

One morning, Sam heard loud, strange snoring from his brother **Ryan's** room. Ryan's heart had stopped working properly.

Sam **called 000**. The call-taker told him to do **CPR**. Sam had learnt CPR at school.

Sam kept going for about **10 minutes**. Then the paramedics came.

Ambulance Victoria said Sam **saved his brother's life**.

Sam made the call. He **stayed on the line**. He **did what the call-taker said**.
body.core:
One morning in 2024, **Sam Bellman**, a 16-year-old student at Warrnambool College, heard strange, loud snoring coming from his brother **Ryan's** room. Something was very wrong. Ryan had gone into **cardiac arrest**: his heart had stopped working properly.

Sam **called 000**. The call-taker told him to start **CPR** (pushing hard and fast on the chest). Sam had learnt CPR at school not long before.

He kept going for about **10 minutes**, until paramedics arrived. Ambulance Victoria said he did **“high quality CPR”**, and that he saved his brother's life.

Sam didn't need a perfect script. He needed to make the call, answer the questions, **stay on the line** and **do what the call-taker said**.
body.extend:
In 2024, **Sam Bellman**, a 16-year-old Warrnambool College student, heard what he described as “death-like” snoring from his brother **Ryan's** room one morning. Ryan had gone into **cardiac arrest**.

Sam **called 000**, and the call-taker instructed him to begin **CPR**. He had learnt the technique at school only recently. Sam kept up chest compressions for about **10 minutes** until paramedics arrived; Ambulance Victoria described it as **“high quality CPR”** and credited him with saving Ryan's life.

The case flips the usual pattern of a phone call. Sam didn't need to plan or perform. The call-taker led; Sam's job was to give clear answers, **stay on the line**, listen closely and **follow spoken instructions** under enormous pressure.

teacher.overview: Students learn that a phone call is a short, structured spoken text (who, why, check, close), practise clarifying and repeating back, adjust formality for the listener, and use their voice clearly. They write a voicemail, plan a 000 call using the school's address, and study a real Warrnambool case where a 16-year-old called 000 and followed the call-taker's CPR instructions. The final task is a real or role-played call.
prep: Arrange with the school office for staff to play receptionist for short role-play calls (by far the best option). Or pair students.
Decide how calls will be recorded (school devices, voice memo) and where recordings are stored.
Optional: install the Emergency+ app on a class device to show how it finds your location.
Print the school's address for the 000 page.

lessons.title: Lesson 1 — The pattern
steps: **Hook (10 min):** play (or act out) a bad call and a good call to a business. What made the difference?
**Explicit teaching (10 min):** model the four steps with the call plan, thinking aloud about formality and repeating back.
**Read (15 min):** article and Check your reading.
**Annotate (10 min):** Anatomy of a phone call.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — Voice and checking
steps: **Voice warm-up (10 min):** say a phone number fast, then in groups. Spell your name aloud. What's easier to catch?
**Make it phone-ready (15 min):** rewrite and read aloud.
**Check it: repeat it back (15 min):** in pairs, one reads the receptionist line, one responds.
**Voicemail (10 min):** write and say it aloud.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — 000
steps: **Explicit teaching (10 min):** what a 000 call-taker asks, and why location comes first. Show the Emergency+ app.
**Plan a 000 call (15 min):** using the school's address. Practise with a pretend phone only.
**Case study (20 min):** Sam stayed on the line. Discuss: what would you need to know to do what Sam did?
**Exit (5 min):** the cross street or landmark nearest your home (not the address).

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — Make the call
steps: **Calls (25 min):** role-plays with the office or a partner; record if possible.
**Review + reflect (10 min):** How did the call go?, quick check, request sign-off.

teacher.answers:
**Four steps:** who, why, check, close. **Voicemail:** name, number (slowly), why you called, what you'd like them to do, number again. **000:** police, fire or ambulance; then where you are (state and suburb or town, then address, cross street or landmark); stay on the line because they may give instructions and need to keep in touch.

**Call plan:** 1 who; 2 why; 3 answer (details ready); 4 ask; 5 repeat back (check day, time, name); 6 close.

**Make it phone-ready (samples):** Sorry, could you say that again, please? / My number is 0412 345 678 (slowly, in groups). / Could I please speak to the manager? / I called on Monday about my order and haven't heard back. Could you help me with that, please?

**Check it:** e.g. *Could I please have the 14th at quarter past three? So that's the 14th at 3:15?* / *So that's Thursday, wearing black, and I ask for Mel?* / *Sorry, could I get your name again, please?* / Call the business's number from its website, or wait and listen for a second message.

**Case study:** Sam called 000, answered the questions, followed the call-taker's instruction to do CPR for about 10 minutes until paramedics arrived. Staying on the line meant he got instructions and help could find them.

realityCheck: **Phone anxiety is real.** For some students this is the hardest course on the map. Never force a real call: a role-play counts as evidence, and they can work up to a real one.
**Never practise by dialling 000.** Use a pretend phone. Use the school's address on the 000 page, not home addresses, for privacy.
**The best partner is the school office.** A short, prearranged role-play with a real receptionist is authentic and safe. Ask them first: it takes about two minutes a student.
**The case study involves a cardiac arrest.** Some students may have lived through a family emergency. Give a heads-up, and keep the focus on what Sam did well.

**Access matters.** Students with hearing or speech differences can use the 106 text emergency service and the National Relay Service; students with family members who don't speak English can say *Police*, *Fire* or *Ambulance* and stay on the line for an interpreter.
**Works in a real class:** yes. Low-tech, and the payoff is immediate: students often make a real call they've been avoiding.
